questions.q: What does this lesson say makes an integration landscape diagram do 'real work' instead of just looking impressive?
options: Labeling every connection with its actual mechanism (such as 'nightly SFTP batch, both directions, with reconciliation'), not just drawing a generic line
Using as many colors as possible
Showing only the Salesforce org with no other systems
Omitting all external APIs to keep the diagram simple
questions.explain: A connection labeled with its actual mechanism tells the reader something true and specific about the design; an unlabeled generic line conveys nothing beyond 'these two things are connected somehow.'

questions.q: Why should the integration diagram show the hub-and-spoke pattern from Lesson 13 rather than twelve point-to-point lines?
options: Because point-to-point lines are visually impossible to draw
Because Lesson 13 was never actually implemented in this design
Because the diagram has to match the actual design, which rejected point-to-point integration in favor of a central hub — drawing point-to-point lines would misrepresent the architecture
Because hub-and-spoke diagrams require fewer total systems
questions.explain: Since Lesson 13 deliberately chose a hub over point-to-point connections, the diagram needs to visually reflect that chosen architecture accurately, not just gesture at a design that isn't the one actually built.

questions.q: Why does the security and sharing diagram show external-user sharing sets as a separate track rather than merging dealers and end customers into the internal role hierarchy tree?
options: Because external users have no visibility into any Salesforce data at all
Because it visually reinforces Lesson 11's point that dealers and end customers are never placed inside the internal hierarchy at all
Because sharing sets are a deprecated Salesforce feature
Because the internal role hierarchy diagram cannot include more than ten boxes
questions.explain: Keeping external-user sharing visually distinct from the internal hierarchy matches the actual design decision from Lesson 11 — a dealer should never be a hierarchy step away from another dealer's data, and the diagram should make that visible.

questions.q: Why does this lesson keep the integration diagram and the security diagram as two separate artifacts rather than combining them?
options: Because Salesforce technically prohibits combining diagram types
Because combined diagrams are always factually incorrect
Because integration and security have no real relationship to each other in this design
Because they convey fundamentally different kinds of information (data flow vs. visibility), and combining them would make neither story read clearly
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a usability decision: a reader asking an integration question wants an uncluttered integration diagram, and a reader asking a security question wants the reverse — the technical architecture document is where the connections between the two get explained in prose.

questions.q: What test does this lesson propose for whether a diagram is actually useful?
options: Whether someone who has never read the earlier lessons could look at it and correctly state, within a minute, what it's showing
Whether it contains at least twenty labeled elements
Whether it uses the same color scheme as the data model diagram
Whether a board member can redraw it from memory afterward
questions.explain: The lesson's standard is that a diagram requiring the earlier lessons' prose to be meaningful has failed at being a diagram — a useful diagram should stand on its own for a new reader.
